title: Paediatric Child Health 2019
subject: Paediatrics
summary: A concise guide for Year‑4 students on common paediatric conditions in East African low‑resource settings, focusing on clinical reasoning, diagnosis, and pragmatic management.

sections.p: Child health refers to the medical care of infants, children and adolescents, with emphasis on prevention, early detection and treatment of common illnesses.
Severity is graded by clinical presentation, vital signs and laboratory markers, guiding urgency of intervention.
b: Mild – stable vitals, no organ dysfunction
Moderate – signs of dehydration or mild shock
Severe – organ failure or life‑threatening complications

sections.p: In low‑resource East Africa, infections dominate, followed by nutritional deficiencies and endemic diseases.
b: Infectious: malaria, bacterial sepsis, diarrhoea, pneumonia, HIV
Nutritional: kwashiorkor, marasmus, vitamin A deficiency

sections.p: Symptoms vary by age but common features include fever, lethargy, poor feeding, vomiting, and respiratory distress.
b: Children: cough, diarrhoea, rash, weight loss
Adolescents: fatigue, menstrual irregularities, growth delay

sections.p: Prioritise bedside tests; use laboratory tests when available, recognising limitations.

t.b: Detects Plasmodium antigens – positive confirms malaria, negative rules out in low prevalence
Assesses anaemia, infection (leukocytosis), and thrombocytopenia – abnormal values guide treatment
Elevated in bacterial infection – helps differentiate from viral causes
Detects proteinuria or haematuria – suggests renal involvement or urinary tract infection
Shows infiltrates or effusion – confirms pneumonia or pleural effusion; use if available

sections.p: Urgent signs requiring immediate referral or intervention.
b: Severe dehydration (sunken eyes, delayed capillary refill)

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, provide supportive care and monitor closely.
b: Antibiotics (amoxicillin or ceftriaxone) for bacterial infection
Referral to higher centre for severe cases

sections.p: Ensure continuity of care, immunisation and nutrition.
Differential diagnoses that mimic common presentations.
b: Severe viral gastroenteritis vs bacterial sepsis

sections.p: Lab or clinical findings that may be falsely normal or abnormal in this setting.
b: Low haemoglobin may be normal in chronic disease
CRP can be normal in early bacterial infection
Malaria rapid test false negative in low parasitaemia

faq.q: What is the first step in managing a child with suspected malaria?
faq.a: Confirm with a rapid diagnostic test; if positive, start antimalarial therapy immediately.

faq.q: How do you differentiate bacterial from viral pneumonia on exam?
faq.a: Look for high fever, productive cough, tachypnoea, and chest indrawing; bacterial pneumonia often has more pronounced signs.

faq.q: Why is vitamin A given to children with measles?
faq.a: It reduces mortality by improving immune function and mucosal integrity.

exam: A 6‑month‑old presents with fever and poor feeding. What is the next best investigation? — Rapid malaria test; if negative, consider bacterial sepsis and obtain full blood count.
A 4‑year‑old has cough and chest indrawing. What antibiotic is first line? — Amoxicillin or ampicillin for uncomplicated pneumonia; consider ceftriaxone if severe.
A 12‑year‑old with weight loss and night sweats is suspected of TB. What is the initial diagnostic step? — Sputum microscopy or GeneXpert; if unavailable, chest X‑ray and clinical assessment.
A child with diarrhoea has sunken eyes and delayed capillary refill. What is the immediate management? — Start IV fluids with isotonic saline and monitor urine output.
A 2‑year‑old has jaundice and hepatomegaly. What is the most likely cause in this setting? — Hepatitis B infection; confirm with serology if possible.
A 10‑year‑old presents with pallor and easy bruising. What is the first laboratory test? — Full blood count to assess haemoglobin and platelet levels.
A child with fever and rash has a positive rapid malaria test but no other signs of infection. What is the next step? — Treat malaria and observe; if rash persists, consider dengue or viral exanthem.
A 3‑year‑old has persistent vomiting and lethargy. What red flag indicates urgent referral? — Persistent vomiting >24h or signs of dehydration (sunken eyes, delayed capillary refill).
